title: The Sleeper Effect
description: A message from an untrustworthy source can gain power after you forget who said it.

sections.title: Quick Understanding
sections.content: A claim from a dubious source is dismissed at first. But the source fades from memory faster than the claim, so weeks later the idea survives — with its credibility problem stripped away.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Memory stores the message and its source separately. The link between them decays quicker than the content, so a discounted claim can quietly become accepted.

sections.title: Real-Life Examples
content: A rumour you dismissed because of who told you resurfaces later as "something you heard".
The claim in a dubious advertisement outlives any memory of the advertisement.

sections.title: What It Looks Like
content: You remember the fact but not where it came from.
A claim that was once obviously biased now feels neutral.

sections.title: Ethical Uses
sections.content: There is no tactic here — this is a memory quirk. Being aware of it is the defence.

sections.title: Manipulative Uses
sections.content: Seeding a claim through a low-credibility channel, expecting the audience to forget the source and keep the message.

sections.title: Red Flags
content: A strong claim with no traceable origin.
You cannot say who first told you this.

sections.title: Defense Strategies
content: Record where you learned a claim, not just the claim itself.
Re-check important beliefs against sources rather than memory.

sections.title: Mistakes People Make
content: Believing that dismissing a source also deletes the message.
Trusting a claim simply because it feels familiar and unattributed.

sections.title: Key Lessons
content: Attribution is fragile; content is sticky.
